podcast.title: Behind-the-Scenes Production
podcast.body: Much of the high-quality sound on The Teenagers' records was attributed to session saxophone player Jimmy Wright, not the group members or producer George Goldner. Wright ended up doing the arrangements for all of their records and was responsible for the distinctive bass intros performed by Sherman Garns. "Much of the work to make the record sound that good was done, not by the teenagers or by Goldner, but by the Session Saxophone player Jimmy Wright, who ended up doing the arrangements on all of the teenagers' records."

podcast.title: Commercial Success Despite Cover Versions
podcast.body: The Teenagers' version of "Why Do Fools Fall in Love" reached number 6 on the pop charts, outperforming an almost immediately released white cover version by the Canadian group The Diamonds, which only went to number 12. This indicated a changing market where the "novelty sound" of a young boy singing in falsetto was more appealing than adult cover artists. "But in a sign of how the times were changing, the Diamond's version of the song only went to number 12, while the teenagers version went to number 6."

podcast.title: Discovery by Richie Barrett
podcast.body: The group's career changed dramatically when Richie Barrett heard them singing on a street corner. Barrett, known for his 1962 single "Some Other Guy" and then the lead singer of The Valentines, was working as a talent scout and producer for George Goldner at Rama Records, a role akin to Ike Turner for Chess or Jesse Stone for Atlantic. "But everything changed for the group, when Richie Barrett heard them singing on a street corner near him."

podcast.title: Exploitation and Lack of Financial Gain
podcast.body: The story of Frankie Lymon and the Teenagers is a cautionary tale of young people of color achieving massive musical success but making no money from their work due to wealthy businessmen, like Morris Levy, who stole their intellectual property and used mafia connections to prevent legal action. "a story of young people of colour having their work become massively successful and making no money off it because of wealthy businessmen stealing their work."

podcast.title: Formation and Early Names
podcast.body: The group began when two Black teenagers from New York, Jimmy Merchant and Sherman Garns, left their previous vocal group, The Earth Angels (named after The Penguins' song). They then teamed up with two Latino neighbors, Joe Negroni and Herman Santiago. They initially called themselves The Hermans, later changing to The Coop Devils in honor of The Cadillacs, and then to The Premiers before becoming The Teenagers. "The Teenagers started when two black teenagers from New York, Jimmy Merchant and Sherman Garns, left the vocal group they'd formed... and hooked up with two Latino neighbours, Joe Negroni and Herman Santiago."

podcast.title: Later Reunions and Members' Deaths
podcast.body: The Teenagers briefly reunited with Frankie Lymon in 1965, but with little success. In the 1970s, they reunited again, briefly including Lymon's brother in the lineup. Sherman Garns passed away in 1977, followed by Joe Negroni in 1978. Herman Santiago and Jimmy Merchant continued performing with various iterations of The Teenagers, with Santiago still active today and Merchant remaining with the band until his retirement a few years prior. "The other Teenagers would reunite, with Lyman's brother joining them briefly, in the 70s."

podcast.title: Name Change by George Goldner
podcast.body: When their debut record was released, it was credited to "The Teenagers featuring Frankie Lymon," rather than The Premiers. George Goldner disliked their prior name and decided to emphasize their youth, particularly that of their new lead singer, Frankie Lymon, as their main selling point. "When the record came out, it wasn't credited to the premieres, but to the teenagers featuring Frankie Leimon."

podcast.title: Post-Lymon Struggles and Lineup Changes
podcast.body: After Frankie Lymon left, The Teenagers struggled to regain their success. They introduced several new lead singers, including Billy LeBvano, a white kid who sounded like Freddie Houston, and even tried focusing on other original members, performing as "Sherman and the Teenagers." Unable to replicate their original sound, they eventually brought in a female singer, Sandra Doyle, before ultimately splitting up in 1961. "The teenage just didn't fare much better. They went through several new lead singers."

podcast.title: Record Label's Decision to Separate Lymon
podcast.body: The record label made the unusual decision to promote Frankie Lymon as a solo star, separating him from The Teenagers, rather than maintaining a successful group. The presumed calculation was to create two hit acts, but neither Lymon nor The Teenagers had another hit after the split. "The record label soon decided that Lyman needed to become a solo star, rather than just being the lead singer of the teenagers."

podcast.title: Songwriting Origin from Love Letters
podcast.body: The group used to practice in the hallway of Sherman Garns' apartment block. A neighbor, annoyed by their repetitive singing, offered them his girlfriend's love letters, some written as poems, suggesting they turn them into songs. This led to the creation of "Why Do Fools Fall in Love" from the phrase "wider bird sing so gay." "The neighbour decided to bring out some love letters his girlfriend had written, some of which were in the form of poems and say to the kids, why don't you turn some of these into songs?"
